summary: The paper measures a known single-learner classification filter for logistic regression: samples whose label disagrees with the out-of-fold prediction are dropped and the model is refit once, on digits and breast cancer with clean labels and 20% or 40% symmetric noise over 5 seeds. Under noise most drops are mislabeled, mean test accuracy is above unfiltered logistic regression in all four noisy settings (not significantly in one) but below clean-label training, and the mean cost on clean labels is a fraction of a point. The authors claim no new method.
strengths: The claims are scoped with unusual care. The paper states that it proposes no new method, names classification filtering and confident learning as close relatives, and claims no advantage over methods it did not run.

Checking every drop against the injected flips gives a useful diagnostic view (drop precision, drop recall, mislabeled share left in the kept set, correct samples lost) that test accuracy alone would hide.
The cost of filtering on clean labels is measured next to the noisy settings, which answers a question a user faces when the noise level is unknown.

Weak cases are reported plainly: the small recovery on breast cancer at 40%, the unstable per-seed recovery on breast cancer at 20%, and the fact that the MLP gap does not isolate the effect of filtering.

The setup is small and easy to follow (scikit-learn datasets, one pass, fixed settings, seed-paired comparisons), and Figure 1 shows the pipeline, the composition of the drops and the gain against the clean-label reference in one place.

weaknesses.issue: The paper never says what was unknown. The abstract goes from 'a known remedy' to 'we measure', and the second paragraph of the introduction opens with 'We ask' without a reason the answer is needed. By the paper's own account, Brodley and Friedl already evaluated single-algorithm filters at noise levels up to at least thirty percent and reported a trade-off between good data discarded and bad data retained across filter types, which are close to the quantities in Table 1. The stated additions (kept-set noise, drops on clean labels, share of lost accuracy won back) are listed without saying what a reader learns from them. The first contribution bullet also repeats the second and third, so the list holds two items presented as three. As written, the work reads as a small re-measurement of a 1999 technique.
weaknesses.where: Abstract; Sec. 1, paragraphs 2 and 3 and contribution list; Sec. 2, 'Filtering mislabeled samples'
weaknesses.suggestion: Add one or two sentences in the introduction that name the gap in terms of a decision, for example whether the filter can be left on when one does not know if the labels are noisy, and what to expect from it when they are. In Related Work, say directly which of these quantities the antecedent already reported and which it did not, after checking that paper. Replace the first bullet with a distinct finding (the setting where recovery fails) or cut the list to two items.

weaknesses.issue: The take-away is weaker and vaguer than the data support. The italic claim and the abstract say the filter 'wins back only part of the lost accuracy'. Almost any imperfect remedy would fit that sentence, and it merges 66 to 78% in three settings with 22% in the fourth (Table 1). The observation most useful to a practitioner (higher accuracy than the unfiltered model in all noisy runs but one, a mean clean-label cost of a fraction of a point, and no need to know the noise rate) is not drawn as the conclusion. It is absent from the italic claim, and the Discussion mentions the cleaner training set and the gap to clean labels but neither the gain over logistic regression nor the small clean-label cost.
weaknesses.where: Abstract; Sec. 1, italic claim; Sec. 5, first paragraph
weaknesses.suggestion: State the central claim with its two regimes: on seed means, much of the lost accuracy returns on digits at both rates and on breast cancer at 20% (the latter gain not established and unstable across seeds), and only a small part returns on breast cancer at 40%. Pair it with the small clean-label cost, and say in the Discussion when, within these settings, a user can expect the filter to help and when it helps little. Quote at most one headline number in the abstract.

weaknesses.issue: The evidence is too narrow to guide a choice, and the relevance to a CVPR audience is not argued. There are two small scikit-learn datasets, both with very accurate clean-label logistic regression, symmetric noise only, no other noise treatment (and no stronger regularization), and no random-drop, oracle or in-sample control. A reader cannot tell whether to prefer this filter over anything else, or whether the gain comes from removing the right samples. The limitations paragraph lists these gaps but does not say what the study is still good for, and the introduction opens on a generic practitioner with no link to vision.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 1, paragraph 1; Sec. 4, 'Methods'; Sec. 5, 'Limitations and next steps'
weaknesses.suggestion: Without claiming transfer, say who in vision fits linear classifiers on small, noisily labeled sets and that those cases were not tested. Present the study explicitly as a baseline measurement in a favorable setting (accurate base model, class-independent noise) against which the listed controls and methods should be compared, and say why symmetric noise is likely the easier case for a disagreement filter, marked as an expectation and not a result. The controls themselves need new runs, and the contribution will stay limited without them.

weaknesses.issue: The most informative reading of the existing data is left implicit. For a correctly labeled sample, a drop means the check model was wrong about the true label, so 'Correct dropped' measures the check model's error directly. The share of such drops is small on clean labels and larger under noise, largest on breast cancer at 40%, where recall is also lowest. For the two-class task, one minus recall is the same error measured on the flipped samples. The paragraph 'Heavier noise costs the filter on both sides' reports the two trends as separate facts and gives no insight into why the weak case is weak.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.1, 'Heavier noise costs the filter on both sides'; Table 1, 'Correct dropped' and 'Drop recall'
weaknesses.suggestion: Add two sentences that read these rows as the error of the out-of-fold check itself: on seed means the model doing the checking gets worse as noise grows, which shows up both as lost correct samples and, on the two-class task, as surviving flips. Link this to the large mislabeled share kept on breast cancer at 40%. The paragraph on chance can then shrink to one sentence, since random removal is a very low bar.

weaknesses.issue: The MLP comparison takes space and adds nothing to the question. The run-in head 'A larger model does not make filtering unnecessary here' asserts something about filtering, while the paragraph ends by saying that the gap says nothing about what filtering adds or about larger models, because unfiltered logistic regression also beats the MLP in every noisy run. A reader who skims the heads takes away more than the body allows.
weaknesses.suggestion: Either drop the MLP from the text and table, or re-head the paragraph with what the runs do show (this untuned MLP is less accurate than logistic regression under noise) and remove the sentence in 'Methods' that motivates it as a test of whether filtering is unnecessary.

weaknesses.issue: A full paragraph of a 4-page paper goes to the significance of the remaining gap to clean-label training (p = 0.053 against 0.049, then 'all four gap verdicts as tentative'). No reader expects a one-pass filter to match clean labels exactly, and the verdicts end up uninformative. What matters is the size of the gap, which Table 2 shows to be under 2 points at the lower rate, about 4 points on digits at 40% and far larger on breast cancer at 40%. That paragraph does not say so.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.2, 'The clean-label reference is not reached'
weaknesses.suggestion: Compress to one or two sentences that describe how the size of the gap differs across settings, citing Table 2 and Fig. 1c, with one remark that the tests are tentative. Use the freed lines for the introduction sentence on what was unknown and for the check-model reading above.

weaknesses.issue: Calling the filter 'ours' (Table 2, the Fig. 1c legend, and as a noun in sentences such as 'Ours has a higher mean accuracy') conflicts with 'We claim no new method' and with the placement against Brodley and Friedl. The title also reads as a method proposal, while the content is a measurement.
weaknesses.where: Title; Sec. 4.2 and 4.3; captions of Table 1 and Table 2; Table 2 row label; Fig. 1c legend and caption
weaknesses.suggestion: Use one descriptive name everywhere, such as 'the filter' or 'out-of-fold filter', including the table row and the figure legend. Consider a title that signals a study of what the filter removes, recovers and costs.

weaknesses.issue: The method argues for the out-of-fold design by memorization ('A model that never saw a sample cannot have memorized a wrong label for it'). No in-sample filter was run, and it is not shown that a regularized linear model memorizes enough here for the distinction to matter, yet the title and the Discussion lean on it.
weaknesses.suggestion: Present this as the usual rationale for held-out filtering, with the citation to the antecedent, and add that these runs do not compare it with an in-sample check.

weaknesses.issue: The evidence for the one analysis of the weak case is split. The flipped-label ranges for the two least accurate seeds sit in the Table 1 caption, the kept-set ranges sit in the text, and neither the table nor the figure marks which seeds are meant. A reader has to assemble the argument from two places.
weaknesses.where: Table 1 caption; Sec. 4.2, 'Breast cancer at the higher rate is the weak case'
weaknesses.suggestion: Move the flipped-label ranges from the caption into the paragraph next to the kept-set ranges, so the caption only explains the table.

weaknesses.issue: The sentence on recomputing numbers and checking references with a software agent pipeline sits in the Statistics paragraph. It is not part of the experiment or the statistical analysis, it distracts from both, and in a blind submission it points to named software and its authors.
weaknesses.suggestion: Remove it from the Statistics paragraph. If a disclosure is required, place it where the venue asks for such statements and keep it compatible with anonymity.

questions: What does a reader learn here that the single-algorithm filter results of Brodley and Friedl did not already show, and did they report any cost on clean labels?
Which vision users do you have in mind for logistic regression on a few hundred to about a thousand noisy samples?
Would a smaller C without any filtering close part of the gap that the filter closes?
Why keep the MLP if unfiltered logistic regression is already ahead of it in every noisy run?
On breast cancer at 40%, is the share won back also small in the three seeds with fewer flipped labels, or is the seed-mean figure driven by the other two?
